[MUQATIL:53:23-25/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | During a public recitation of Surat al-Najm, Satan put a phrase praising the exalted cranes and hoped-for intercession on Muhammad's tongue; Meccan polytheists rejoiced and hoped for angelic intercession.
[MUQATIL:53:23-25/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | At the surah's end, Muhammad and the believers prostrated in affirmation of God, while Meccan polytheists prostrated at the idols; the elderly Walid ibn al-Mughira prostrated by lifting dirt to his forehead.
[MUQATIL:53:23-25/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | After people hoped that angels would intercede, God declared that both the afterlife and this world belong to Him; the author links this to resurrection and recompense. | mentions 6:12, 53:31
[FARRA:v3p99/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The afterlife and the present life, and their reward, belong to God.
[NAHHAS:v4p272/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | God gives whatever He wills to whomever He wills.
[THALABI:v9p147#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Both the afterlife and this world belong to God: He gives what He wills to whom He wills and denies whom He wills.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p399/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | God is more powerful than creatures; were a child possible, He would be more entitled to sons than polytheists, though exalted above their claim.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p399/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | God gives prophethood to His chosen one, not everyone who wishes for it, because He owns heaven and earth.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p250/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The hereafter and this world belong to God as creator and owner; He alone has complete sovereignty, while every creature is inherently deficient.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p49#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Both the afterlife and this world belong to God; no one owns or receives anything from either without His permission, refuting what the unbeliever wishes for.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:53:25-30/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Both the Hereafter and this world belong to God, and nothing occurs in either except by His will.
[JISHUMI:v9p6650/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو علي | prefers | Abu Ali says God grants what benefits people: worldly and afterlife wishes, including religion, wealth, prophethood, and Paradise, but gives the afterlife to deserving believers rather than unbelievers; the author prefers this comprehensive view.
[JISHUMI:v9p6650/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation rejects the idea that a person may do whatever he wishes without recompense: God owns both lives, rewards obedience, and punishes disobedience.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p410/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Both the afterlife and this world belong to God; no one possesses anything in them except by His permission.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p424#2/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | God owns both the hereafter and this world, giving or withholding from either as He wills; no one can dictate anything to Him.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p202/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The Hereafter and this world are the two abodes, both wholly under God's ownership, power, and authority.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p74#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | God alone owns the afterlife and this world; no one controls anything in either without His permission.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-ākhirah modifies either life or abode; al-ākhir is an active participle from an unattested verb, illustrated by أخرته فتأخر, though usage bars the expected form.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-ūlā is the feminine form فعلى, so its masculine أول is an أفعل adjective.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Every أفعل/فعلى pair requires a base; here, as with الآخر, that source form is unattested.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A past action is only truly past when complete; a hypothetical verb yielding آخر would mean reaching completed finality, although every completed action has an end after it.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The form تأخر is a reflexive or effortful claim to being last, not proof of a basic verb that makes someone truly آخر.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | آخر is an active participle without a verb, intensified as أفعل; آخر is a connected part, while الآخر is separate and comes after it.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | الأول has neither a verb nor a participle: an agent must precede an act, so the first cannot itself derive from an act that makes it first.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One explanation: whoever chose a desired deity in worldly life will be punished here or, if not here, in the afterlife; 53:26 confirms that no intercession will avail. | mentions 53:26
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Another explanation: since al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā rest on conjecture and desire, God's ownership shows idols have no authority; 53:26 answers the claim that they are angelic intercessors. | mentions 53:26
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | This may console the Prophet, who had explained his mission and God's unity without being believed: the deniers cannot escape God's power.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | It may be a conclusion from proof: after establishing Muhammad's revelation, including the message of divine unity, God's ownership of both lives confirms his truthful report of resurrection. | mentions 53:4
[RAZI-FULL:v28p261/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | It may answer unbelievers who said believers were not better guided because they lacked worldly wealth: God gives wealth and guidance to whom He wills in either life. | mentions 46:11
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although Arabs use الأولة as feminine of الأول, أولى looks like a comparative whose feminine should not take ة; أول is exceptional, resembling both أربع/أرنب and الأكبر/الأصغر, so أولى is also used.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The forms الأولة and الأولى explain why أولا may appear with or without tanwin: the ة form permits it, while الأولى is diptote.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Qurʾanic feminine الأولى is more common, so the usual form leaves tanwin; Arabs also preserve the etymological أولة, though Rāzī calls it weaker.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A further grammatical proposal is that أفعل is diptote only when its feminine is exclusively فعلى; allowing a ة feminine removes that restriction.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The apparent counterexample from سبق fails: سابق applied to the first is resemblance, since an agent and its act do not compete; تقدم was already answered through تأخر.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Rāzī rejects deriving أول from آل as “making another first” as far-fetched.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | أول and آخر are أفعل/فاعل forms, whereas قبل and بعد are neither forms; the words therefore differ morphologically even when their senses are related.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | آخر requires a specific afterness with nothing further after it; something can follow the first yet remain intermediate rather than last.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The relation is asymmetrical: arriving after everyone explains why someone is last, but being last does not explain every use of “after.”
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Rāzī cites the Prophet's saying, “Do not revile time, for time is God”; he gives no grading.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p262/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Temporal priority and posteriority have reality only through God; without God there would be no temporal order to revile.
[QURTUBI-FULL:53:23-25/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | God owns the first and later life and gives or withholds as He wills, regardless of anyone’s wishes.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:53:23-25/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | God alone owns the Hereafter and this world, giving from either to whomever He wills; no one can dictate to Him.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p190#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | God owns both worlds and rules over them, granting prophethood and intercession to whom He wills and approves, not to whoever merely wishes.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p18/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | God owns the afterlife and this world and gives or withholds from either as He wills; no one attains anything except by His will.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p18/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The afterlife is placed before the present life because it comes later and to fit the verse ending, rather than following chronological order. | mentions 92:13
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p458#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | All affairs belong to God, who owns and governs this world and the next; what He wills happens and what He does not will cannot happen.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p324/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The quoted wish to receive good from God on return is denied: the speaker will not get what he wants, proving his subjection to the sole sovereign. | mentions 41:50
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p324/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The whole dominion belongs to God alone.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p324/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The afterlife is where pleasures, fulfilled wishes, and their deprivation reach full realization; idolaters imagine their gods will intercede and make them prosper there.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p324/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The afterlife is mentioned

 first because only those who follow guidance and resist desire attain their wishes there; nobody attains every wish in worldly life.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p324/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The ordering is semantic, not for rhyme, since al-ukhrā would also have suited the rhyme.
[ITQAN:v3p37/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The reversed order “Hereafter and this world” is chosen to preserve the verse ending; the same concern shapes “We gathered you and the earlier peoples.” | mentions 77:38
[BURSEVI:v9p194/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God's exclusive ownership of both afterlife and present world explains why a person is not guaranteed the fulfillment of every wish.
[ALUSI-FULL:v27p58#3/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | This explains the preceding denial: God alone owns all affairs of the afterlife and this world, so humans have no independent control; what God wills occurs, and what He does not will does not.
[ALUSI-FULL:v27p58#3/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The afterlife is mentioned first because rebutting the opponents' hope of winning there is especially important; the next verse follows from this point.
[ELMALILI:53:23-25#2/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The first and final life both belong to God: human existence begins by His will, and the afterlife unfolds under His rule and law.
[ELMALILI:53:23-25#2/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | To attain one's final good, one must follow the proofs and rules God revealed rather than relying on personal wishes; bare idealism is insufficient without a sound practical basis.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p111/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Since God owns the afterlife and this world, He governs their inhabitants by His will, refuting the polytheists’ belief in idol intercession.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p112/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The clause makes explicit the additional restriction implied by the prior verse; fronting for God expresses exclusivity, since the two lives belong to God, not people. | mentions 53:24
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p112/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The afterlife and the first life mean the next world and this world, including all that each contains, as in the reference to the two easts and two wests. | mentions 55:17
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p112/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The afterlife comes first to emphasize its importance and direct believers' concern toward it, while also fitting the verse ending.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p112/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | After denying that people control what they wish, the passage illustrates the point with the idolaters' hope that idols intercede, quoting their claims in 39:3 and 10:18. | mentions 39:3, 10:18
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p112/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Even honored angels cannot intercede unless God permits it and wills to accept the plea for its recipient; idols, mere stones on earth, have still less claim. | mentions 10:18
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p112/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The move to intercession follows the denial that people get all they wish and underscores the gravity of intercession rather than abruptly changing topics. | mentions 53:24
[TABATABAI:53:24-27/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God’s exclusive ownership of this life and the next is the reason people cannot acquire their wishes simply by wishing.
[TABATABAI:53:24-27/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Neither the first life nor the Hereafter has a partner with God in its dominion.
[ASAD-NOTES:53:24#n18/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The particle means despite the fact that God is omnipotent and omniscient, needing no mediator between Himself and His creatures.
[ASAD-NOTES:53:24/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Both the life to come and the present life belong to God alone.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p40/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Idolaters follow conjecture and baseless wishes despite manifest guidance; desire cannot replace truth, and they will face the warned facts rather than what they wish for.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p50/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Reward and punishment are realities, and conjecture or wishes cannot overcome them; all affairs of heaven and earth remain in God's hands.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p54/r8] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The question about attaining desires expresses amazement at, and comments on, the preceding argument: wishes do not determine what reality grants.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p55/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | When reality arrives, false hopes collapse: deities cannot help, and each person is judged by deeds, entering Paradise or Hell according to whether good or evil deeds prevail.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p55/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The warning applies to everyone: Arabs, Jews, Christians, and Muslims also harbor desires invented by fancy; Islahi connects Jewish and Christian amāniyyu to al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān and says Muslims invented beliefs against Qur'an and Sunnah by following them.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p55/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The Qur'an's general word “man” addresses every individual without exception: desires neither change reality nor make God's law biased.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p55/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Anyone expecting God's laws to accommodate personal wishes must know that both worlds belong to God; nobody can intercede or change His laws and decisions without His permission.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:53:19/r22] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Both the afterlife and worldly life depend on God’s will, and intercession likewise cannot be considered independent of that will.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:53:19/r23] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Taberî | reports | Tabari takes ‘the human’ in verse 24 to mean Muhammad, with these and the next verse indicating his high rank came by God’s grace rather than his own wish.
[STUDYQURAN:53:25/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Pagan followers seem to believe in a god and hereafter, but fit them to conjectures and caprices, effectively denying God’s mastery of both worlds.
[STUDYQURAN:53:intro/r14] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The second section reproaches Quraysh for idol worship, discusses its roots in ignorance and conjecture, and condemns seeking angels’ intercession.

<<end of notes>>
